title: the lamps of Diwali
hookLine: Bharata gives back the kingdom, and where Diwali's lamps come from
carry: diwali's lamps welcome the light home
last: TOUCHING FEET: HUMILITY THAT ASKS A BLESSING.

cards: Why are the lamps lit at Diwali? One answer you'll hear from people who grew up with the festival: because Rama came home, and the whole city lit lamps so he could find his way. It's a lovely picture.
So here's a surprise. Open Valmiki's Ramayana to the homecoming and look for the lamps. Valmiki describes flags, flowers, music, roads sprinkled with water, a crowd so big it fills the streets.
A city lit by rows of lamps isn't the picture he paints. The lamps seem to have arrived later, as the story moved into the festival.
Today, what Valmiki does tell: the homecoming itself, and the man at the center of it, who isn't Rama.

teach.b: Bharata never wanted the throne. When the news comes, his joy fills the chapter. He orders the roads leveled and watered, the city decorated, the musicians out.

When the Pushpaka comes into sight, Bharata goes out on foot, carrying the sandals. Rama steps down, Bharata bows, and does what he has waited fourteen years to do: he puts the sandals back on his brother's feet.
The kingdom, he says, was a deposit left with me; I'm giving it back. That's Valmiki's homecoming: a promise kept on both sides. So where do the lamps come from?
Deepavali means a row of lamps.
In much of North India, families light them because Rama came home.
Many also welcome Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune, into a clean, bright house that night, and in much of South India the festival remembers Krishna's victory over the demon Narakasura.
Different stories, one teaching Hindus hand their children: light wins over darkness, and the good is welcomed home. Neighbors light lamps that season too.
Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas, and Jains remember Mahavira's final liberation, each with their own story. Same lamps, their own reasons.

how: On Diwali, Hindu families clean the house, light rows of diyas, often do Lakshmi puja in the evening and share sweets; in much of North India the lamps remember Rama's return, and in much of South India the festival remembers Krishna's victory over Narakasura.

o: the festival of lamps, linked with Rama's homecoming
a coronation feast held when a new king is crowned
a feast for the ancestors held at the new moon

p: welcomed into a clean, bright house

s: Valmiki describes the city lighting rows of lamps for Rama
Valmiki describes flags, flowers, music and watered roads. the lamps came later, with the festival.
Diwali has only one story, Rama's homecoming
many families also welcome Lakshmi, and much of South India remembers Krishna's victory over Narakasura.
Bharata calls the kingdom something left with him for safekeeping
a deposit, he says, and now he gives it back.

games.q: a friend asks what Diwali's lamps are really for. by this week's story, what's the best answer?
o: only for Rama; Valmiki describes them.
light over darkness, the good welcomed home: Rama, Lakshmi and more, by region.
games.why: Valmiki's homecoming has flags and music, not rows of lamps. the festival gathered several stories, and each one welcomes the light home.

practice: If you can, light a diya, a candle, or a lamp by a window, the way Hindu homes do on Diwali. As it catches, name one thing you want welcomed into your home this year: patience, a person, peace.
Then name one darkness you'd like it to push back. If you don't pray, simply watch the flame for a minute and let the two names settle.

wordCard.voice: Diwali. Deepavali, a row of lamps. In Valmiki the homecoming is Bharata's day; in the festival, the lamps welcome the light home.

orig.note: Sanskrit dīpāvalī: dīpa (lamp) + āvalī (row); Diwali is its everyday form.

carryVoice: Your line: diwali's lamps welcome the light home. Bharata kept the trust; the lamps came later. Until tomorrow.
